# Gym asteroids do not drop minerals — share the mineral kill-drop code with the game

## Headline

Gym asteroids do not drop minerals because the kill-drop rule lives only in the
game (`PlayScene`) while the gyms run a divergent copy. Extract the rule into one
shared helper used by both, and wire it into the gyms so they drop minerals
(small-asteroid single drop; non-asteroid 25–50 % re-drop) exactly as the game
does.

## Problem statement

Asteroids in the gym scenes do not drop minerals when destroyed, even though the
shipped game does and the gyms' own documentation says they should. The cause is
code divergence: the mineral **kill-drop** logic lives privately in `PlayScene`
and was never shared, while the gyms re-implemented the collection half of the
mineral layer and omitted the drop half. The fix is to make gym asteroids drop
minerals (per GDD §4.4.1) and to move the kill-drop logic into a single shared
helper used by both the game and the gyms, so the two can no longer drift.

## Users

- **As a player using the minerals gym**, when I destroy a small asteroid I want
  it to leave a mineral, so the gym demonstrates the real mechanic I see in the
  game.
- **As a player using the asteroid enemy gym**, when I destroy a small asteroid
  I want it to drop a mineral, so the gym matches the game's asteroid behaviour.
- **As a developer**, I want the mineral kill-drop logic to exist in exactly one
  shared place, so a gym and the game can never again disagree about whether an
  asteroid drops a mineral.
- **As a player**, when a non-asteroid enemy that has absorbed minerals is
  destroyed, I want it to re-drop a fraction of them, in the gym as in the game.

## Root cause (RCA summary)

- The shared base `src/scenes/core/CombatScene.ts` provides the generic
  destruction seam (`onPlayerBulletHitsEnemy` → `onEnemyDestroyed`) but has no
  mineral concept.
- `src/scenes/PlayScene.ts` overrides `onEnemyDestroyed` and, in the private
  `_onEnemyKilled()`, implements the drops: small asteroid → `spawnMineralAt()`;
  large/medium asteroid → none (split children drop); non-asteroid enemy →
  `entity.spawnMineralDrops()` (25–50 % re-drop).
- `src/scenes/gym/core/GymFormationScene.ts` re-implements the mineral layer
  (`seedMinerals`, `_initMineralLayer`, `_updateMinerals`) but its
  `onEntityDestroyed` path only splits asteroids — it never spawns a mineral and
  never calls `spawnMineralDrops()` on death.
- `GymMinerals.ts` (asteroids-only) and `GymEnemies.ts` (generic enemy gym, used
  for the "Asteroid" config row) both extend `GymFormationScene`, so both are
  affected.
- Prior unification work (AH-0MUD8E015004C4JO) shared the combat core but left
  the mineral logic duplicated — exactly the divergence the operator suspected.
- The gym docstrings and GDD §6.4 already claim "small-asteroid mineral drops …
  enemy absorption/re-drop"; the earlier gym item (AH-0MUCST5HA0079APB) had this
  in its acceptance criteria but it was closed without the drop behaviour.

## Existing state

- `BaseEnemy.mineralRedropCount()` / `spawnMineralDrops()` already implement the
  25–50 % re-drop and are unit-tested (AH-0MUCST3QD002O9TA / AH-0MUCST1P10004EXM).
- `PlayScene.spawnMineralAt()` is public and used by the game and, in principle,
  by gyms.
- `Asteroid.collectMineral()` is a no-op (asteroids are inert to minerals) and
  `Asteroid.getSizeTier()` / `getSplitChildren()` exist.
- `GymFormationScene` already owns a mineral field, a hold, a HUD counter and the
  hold-full choice overlay, and seeds 100 minerals on create.
- The rules config exposes `mineralCollectAmount`, `mineralHoldCapacity`,
  `mineralRedropFractionMin`/`Max`.

## Desired change

- Extract the mineral kill-drop rule into one shared helper used by **both**
  `PlayScene` and `GymFormationScene` (and therefore every formation gym).
  The helper decides, for a destroyed enemy, how many minerals to spawn and
  where: small asteroid → exactly one at the death site; large/medium asteroid →
  none; non-asteroid enemy → the configured fraction of minerals absorbed,
  scattered at the death site.
- Wire the helper into the gym destruction path so gym asteroids (and other
  gyms' enemies) drop minerals exactly as the game does.
- Leave gameplay values and balance unchanged; reuse the existing rules tunables.
- Keep the game's observable behaviour identical (pure refactor there), and keep
  the existing mineral tests green.

## Acceptance Criteria

- **AC1 — Gyms drop on small-asteroid destruction.** Destroying a small asteroid
  in `GymMinerals` and in the `GymEnemies` asteroid-config row spawns exactly one
  mineral at the asteroid's position (matching `PlayScene`). Large/medium
  asteroids do not drop directly; their small split children do. Verified by a
  scene test that destroys a small asteroid and asserts the live mineral count
  increases by one at that position, and by a test that a large/medium asteroid
  splits without a direct drop.
- **AC2 — Gyms re-drop for non-asteroid enemies.** In a gym, a non-asteroid
  enemy that has absorbed minerals re-drops between the configured
  `mineralRedropFractionMin`/`Max` fraction of them (never more than collected)
  at its death site. Verified by a deterministic test injecting a seeded RNG.
- **AC3 — Single shared code path.** The mineral kill-drop rule (small-asteroid
  drop + non-asteroid re-drop) is implemented once in a shared helper/module and
  consumed by both `PlayScene` and `GymFormationScene`; `PlayScene`'s private
  kill-drop block delegates to it. Verified by a parity/equivalence test and by
  the repo-wide duplicate-body guard passing.
- **AC4 — No game behaviour regression.** `PlayScene` mineral behaviour
  (small-asteroid drop, non-asteroid re-drop, collection, absorption, hold-fill
  choice) is unchanged; the existing `PlayScene` mineral tests stay green.
- **AC5 — Tests are added and green.** New/extended tests cover AC1–AC3 in the
  gym suites (`GymMinerals.test.ts`, `GymEnemies.test.ts`,
  `GymFormationScene.test.ts`) and all pass.
- **AC6 — Documentation updated.** The GDD (§4.4.1 and §6.4), the
  `GymMinerals`/`GymFormationScene` docstrings and any relevant README/docs
  entries describe the shared mineral kill-drop code and the gym behaviour.
- **AC7 — Full project test suite passes.** `npm test` (the full suite) passes
  with the new changes.

## Constraints

- Do not change balance/tuning values; use the existing rules config.
- Prefer a genuinely shared helper over per-scene copies (the operator selected
  the shared-helper approach); avoid introducing a second divergence.
- The extracted helper must not force gym-specific concerns (hold, HUD, choice)
  into the game, nor game-specific concerns (score, waves) into the gym.
- Tests must be meaningful and deterministic (TDD preferred); no snapshot-only
  or trivially-true assertions.
- Written output and docs in UK English.

## Key Files (predicted)

- `src/scenes/core/CombatScene.ts` — likely host for, or hook to, the shared
  mineral kill-drop helper (shared base of game and gyms).
- `src/scenes/core/<new mineral helper>.ts` (or `src/core/minerals.ts`) — the
  single shared implementation of the kill-drop rule.
- `src/scenes/PlayScene.ts` — refactor `_onEnemyKilled()` mineral block to
  delegate to the shared helper (no behaviour change).
- `src/scenes/gym/core/GymFormationScene.ts` — call the shared helper from the
  destruction path; add dropped minerals to the gym's mineral field.
- `src/entities/BaseEnemy.ts` — reuse `spawnMineralDrops()` / `mineralRedropCount()`.
- `src/entities/Asteroid.ts` — reuse `getSizeTier()` / `getSplitChildren()`.
- `src/scenes/gym/GymMinerals.test.ts`, `src/scenes/gym/GymEnemies.test.ts`,
  `src/scenes/gym/core/GymFormationScene.test.ts`,
  `src/scenes/__tests__/PlayScene.minerals.test.ts` — tests.
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — §4.4.1 / §6.4 wording and gym docstrings.

## Related work

- `AH-0MUBVGI62004ED9Q` — parent mechanic (asteroids drop minerals; hold; choice).
- `AH-0MUCST5HA0079APB` — asteroids-only mineral gym; its AC claimed small-asteroid
  drops and enemy re-drop, but the drop half was not implemented (this item closes
  that gap).
- `AH-0MUD8E015004C4JO` — prior unification of PlayScene/GymFormationScene combat
  logic into a shared core; this item extends the same principle to minerals.
- `AH-0MUCST3QD002O9TA` — mineral rules tunables and per-enemy mineral count.
- `AH-0MUCST1P10004EXM` — tests for enemy mineral count and re-drop distribution.
- `AH-0MUCST3BS0007CPT` — Mineral collectable entity and constants.
- `AH-0MUHMXWGC0058BO4` — ability items (Dual Shot/Teleport/Phase Shift) not
  functioning; a distinct gym-sharing defect, not a mineral drop issue.
- `AH-0MUHM66ES0027QQV` — enemy gym P3/P6 hit-gating not shared; a distinct
  gym-sharing defect, not a mineral drop issue.

## Out of scope

- Fixing the distinct gym-sharing defects `AH-0MUHMXWGC0058BO4` (ability items)
  and `AH-0MUHM66ES0027QQV` (enemy gym P3/P6 hit-gating).
- Any change to mineral balance/tuning values or the hold/choice reward pool.
- Reworking the reward/choice flow itself; only the drop-on-kill wiring changes.

## Risks and assumptions

- **Risk:** the clean shared boundary is unclear because the game and gyms differ
  in hold/HUD/choice/score concerns. **Mitigation:** share only the field +
  collection/absorption + kill-drop mechanics, keep hold/score/choice in the
  scenes, and cover the seam with parity tests.
- **Risk:** scope creep into the two related gym-sharing defects
  (`AH-0MUHMXWGC0058BO4`, `AH-0MUHM66ES0027QQV`). **Mitigation:** keep those out
  of scope; they are separate work items.
- **Risk:** the refactor could change `PlayScene` behaviour subtly.
  **Mitigation:** AC4 requires the existing mineral tests to remain green and a
  parity test to pin the shared rule.
- **Assumption:** gyms should behave exactly like the game for mineral drops
  (operator confirmed the non-asteroid re-drop should be included).
- **Assumption:** the shared helper is the preferred approach over a local gym
  patch (operator selected the shared helper).

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- Q: "Non-asteroid enemy re-drop in gyms — include it, or asteroids only?" —
  **Answer (operator):** "Yes, include it." Source: interactive reply. Context:
  the re-drop mechanism already exists (`BaseEnemy.spawnMineralDrops`) but is not
  wired into gyms; including it keeps the shared path complete.
- Q: "Refactor boundary — shared helper used by both PlayScene and
  GymFormationScene, or a local gym patch?" — **Answer (operator):** "Shared
  helper." Source: interactive reply. Context: RCA confirms the divergence, so a
  shared helper prevents recurrence.
- Q (operator-initiated): "Check whether a work item exists for the previously
  raised issue about enemy drops; if so, close it." — **Answer/Research:** no
  open work item matching "enemy drops" exists in the worklog. All drop/mineral
  items are already `completed` (`AH-0MUBVGI62004ED9Q`, `AH-0MUCST5HA0079APB`,
  `AH-0MUCST1P10004EXM`, `AH-0MUCST3QD002O9TA`, etc.). The only related *open*
  items are `AH-0MUHMXWGC0058BO4` (ability items) and `AH-0MUHM66ES0027QQV`
  (enemy gym hit-gating), both distinct defects and left open. No item closed.

## Related work (automated report)

### Related work items
- **AH-0MUA8BK1E001UZUC** – Apply rebindable keys to gameplay and menus (completed)
- **AH-0MUGCSQKU003R4WW** – Update documentation — asteroid spawn mechanic (completed)
- **AH-0MT7QQGBU008V4R0** – Write the Game Design Document (completed)

### Repository file matches
- `README.md` — matched: asteroid, asteroids, code, destruction, diverge (+31 more)
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — matched: asteroid, asteroids, code, destruction, diverge (+27 more)
- `docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md` — matched: asteroid, asteroids, code, destruction, diverge (+25 more)

## Plan: decomposition (2026-09-26)

**Pre-check:** effort Small / risk Medium → planning required (`plan_helpers.py plan-if-needed` → `decision: plan`). Plan-approval gate → `request_approval: false` (risk Medium is below the gate's High threshold), so no approval pause was required; the plan proceeded straight to the automated review stages.

### Child work items (dependency-ordered, test-first)

| # | Work item | Type | Depends on |
|---|-----------|------|------------|
| 1 | Test: shared mineral kill-drop rule — `AH-0MUIG1AFG00938TV` | task | — |
| 2 | Shared mineral kill-drop helper + PlayScene/BaseEnemy refactor — `AH-0MUIGTRFY002JDDS` | task | 1 |
| 3 | Test: gyms drop minerals on kill — `AH-0MUIGTRVA0072TWW` | task | 2 |
| 4 | Wire gyms to the shared mineral kill-drop helper — `AH-0MUIGTSAX00096Y4` | task | 3 |
| 5 | Documentation update + full-suite verification — `AH-0MUIG16QK003MSNO` | docs | 4 |

The dependency graph is a verified DAG (test → impl → test → impl → docs/verify). Test/verification items precede their implementation items.

### AC traceability (parent AC → child items)

- **AC1 (gyms drop on small-asteroid destruction):** 3, 4
- **AC2 (gyms re-drop for non-asteroid enemies):** 3, 4
- **AC3 (single shared code path):** 1, 2, 4
- **AC4 (no game behaviour regression):** 2
- **AC5 (tests added and green):** 1, 3
- **AC6 (documentation updated):** 4, 5
- **AC7 (full project test suite passes):** 5

Coverage review (`tree_coverage.py run-coverage-review`): `recommendation: proceed`, 100 % of parent ACs covered.

### Design decisions & assumptions (documented, not open questions)

- **Shared helper location:** `src/scenes/core/mineralKillDrops.ts` exporting `resolveMineralKillDrops(scene, entity, rng): Mineral[]`, consumed by `PlayScene` and `GymFormationScene`. Rationale: it needs scene/`Mineral`/`Asteroid` types and sits with the shared combat core (`CombatScene`), matching the item's predicted Key Files.
- **Scatter reuse:** `BaseEnemy.spawnMineralDrops()` delegates to the shared scatter maths, keeping its public API and RNG draw order so `PlayScene` behaviour is byte-for-byte identical for non-asteroid re-drops.
- **Gym RNG seam:** `GymFormationScene` gains an injectable scene RNG (default `Math.random`) so gym drop tests are deterministic; configuration already accepts an `rng` for the power-up layer, but a scene-level seam is required for mineral drops.
- **All destruction paths drop once:** the gym drop is invoked from both `onEnemyDestroyed` and `explodeRandom`, so EXPLODE (which bypasses `onEnemyDestroyed`) matches the game's bullet/ram paths without double-dropping.
- Balance/tuning values are unchanged; only the wiring and the shared helper are added.

2. Completeness — all children have a description and a measurable `## Acceptance Criteria`; `**Key Files:**` syntactically validated (`validate_key_files_in_description` → no issues) and checked for scope relevance.

5. Acceptance & testability — all child ACs are pass/fail with an explicit metric (counts, positions, seeded RNG, command outcomes).
6. Polish & handoff — descriptions use UK English, are copy-pasteable, and reference concrete files and commands.

# Test: shared mineral kill-drop rule

Test-first task for AH-0MUHMT5JC004WRSB (AC3, AC5).

## Goal

Write deterministic unit + guard tests that pin the contract of the shared mineral kill-drop rule **before** it is implemented, so `PlayScene` and the gyms provably share one rule.

## Required coverage

- Small asteroid (`getSizeTier() === 'small'`) → exactly one mineral drop at the asteroid's death position.
- Large and medium asteroid → no direct drop (their small split children drop).
- Non-asteroid enemy that absorbed N minerals → re-drops between `mineralRedropFractionMin` and `mineralRedropFractionMax` of N, never more than N, at the death site, using a seeded RNG for determinism.
- Non-asteroid enemy with 0 absorbed minerals → no drops.
- Re-drop scatter stays within `MINERAL_REDROP_SCATTER_RADIUS` of the death site.

## Assumption

Shared helper module path: `src/scenes/core/mineralKillDrops.ts` exporting `resolveMineralKillDrops(scene, entity, rng): Mineral[]` (operator selected the shared-helper approach — see the parent item's Appendix).

## Acceptance Criteria

- **AC3 — Single shared code path.** The mineral kill-drop rule (small-asteroid drop + non-asteroid re-drop) has one production definition that both `PlayScene` and `GymFormationScene` consume, and a repo-wide guard asserts it.
- **AC5 — Tests are added and green.** New tests cover the shared rule and the guard; `npm test` for the new files passes.
- The unit tests are deterministic (seeded RNG, no reliance on `Math.random`) and cover every bullet under Required coverage.
- Tests fail before the implementation task lands and pass once it does.

## Key Files

- `src/scenes/core/mineralKillDrops.test.ts` — new.
- `src/scenes/core/CombatScene.equivalence.test.ts` — extend guard.
- `src/test/duplicateBodyGuard.ts` — shared guard helper (extend if needed).
- `src/entities/__tests__/BaseEnemy.minerals.test.ts` — keep green / extend.
- `src/scenes/__tests__/PlayScene.minerals.test.ts` — keep green / extend.

# Intake brief — Gym↔game behavioural-parity audit

**Headline:** A full evaluation of the scene layer found twelve places where the shipped `PlayScene` and the gym scenes still run **divergent copies of the same behaviour**. This epic tracks extracting each into one shared implementation (or explicitly recording an intentional difference), so that every object behaves identically in every scene and new divergence is caught by an automated guard.

## Problem statement

Operators continue to see errors caused by differences between gym scenes and the game scene. The producer directive is that **gyms and the game must execute the same core code**; the only legitimate difference is that a gym enables a **constrained set of features** (one enemy type, the enemy editor, fixed formations, no campaign/wave progression). Prior epics (`AH-0MUD8E015004C4JO`, `AH-0MUDCT7EU0061OSZ`) unified the eight combat/lifecycle methods onto `CombatCoreScene`/`CombatScene`, but the audit below shows that a second tier of behaviour — player control, enemy fire dispatch, projectile lifecycle, power-up drops, minerals, the boss, teleport and the gym base seams — is still duplicated and has already drifted.

## Users

- **As a player**, when I practice in a gym I want every object (player, enemies, asteroids, boss, minerals, power-ups, bullets) to behave exactly as it does in the game, so the gym is a truthful training ground.
- **As a developer**, when I change a behaviour I want to change it in exactly one place, so a scenario cannot drift from the shipped game.
- **As a tester**, I want an automated parity guard that fails when a scene re-introduces a duplicate of a shared method, so regressions are caught before release.
- **As the producer**, I want the "gyms are the parity reference" principle enforced by code structure and tests.

## Evaluation method

Reviewed every production scene under `src/scenes` (`PlayScene`, `GymFormationScene` and its subclasses `GymEnemies`/`GymBoss`/`GymMinerals`, `GymPlayer`, `GymWeapons`, `GymPowerUpsCombat`, `GymPowerUpsUtility`) plus the shared cores `CombatCoreScene`/`CombatScene`, and the entity/config layer (`enemyFactory`, `BaseEnemy`, `Asteroid`, `Boss`, `Mineral`, `powerups/*`). Compared method inventories, dispatch tables, per-frame sequences and copy-pasted bodies, and cross-checked against the existing worklog so as not to duplicate open items.

## Findings — the gap register

| # | Gap | Evidence (divergent copies) | Impact |
|---|-----|------------------------------|--------|
| 1 | **Player-control step duplicated** | Input→timers→multipliers→physics sequence re-implemented in `PlayScene.tick`, `GymFormationScene.tick`, `GymWeapons.tick`, `GymPowerUpsUtility.tick`, `GymPowerUpsCombat.tick`; `GymPlayer.update` inlines the input-map branch instead of the shared `_readPlayerInput` | Player movement/fire-rate differs between scenes; GymPlayer does not share any control code |
| 2 | **Enemy fire dispatch duplicated** | `PlayScene._fireFor` and `GymEnemies.collectBullets` both hard-code `enemyKey → tryFire*`; `GymPowerUpsCombat._tickScouts` re-implements it again with a **fake fixed 16 ms clock** (`_nextFireTime += 16`) instead of the scene clock | A new enemy type must be wired twice; gym/combat fire cadence is frame-count-based, not time-based |
| 3 | **Projectile lifecycle duplicated** | Enemy-bullet wrap+expiry loop in `PlayScene._advanceBullets`, `GymFormationScene.tick`, `GymPowerUpsCombat._advanceEnemyBullets`; player-bullet advance via `advanceAndCull` in `PlayScene`, `GymFormationScene._advancePlayerBullets`, `GymWeapons._advanceBullets`/`advanceBullets` | Wrap/expiry fixes reach one scene only |

| 6 | **Boss integration diverges** | `PlayScene._updateBoss(dt)` runs inside `tick`; `GymBoss.update` calls `super.tick(dt)` **then** advances the boss, so `GymBoss.tick()` never advances the boss; `PlayScene.getAdditionalTeleportBodies` avoids the boss for P7, `GymBoss` does not; `PlayScene._spawnMinions` (phase minions) has no gym equivalent | Boss behaves differently (bullet timing, teleport safety, minions) in the gym |

| 8 | **Asteroid split duplicated** | Identical `onEntityDestroyed` split closures in `GymEnemies.ts` and `GymMinerals.ts` | A split-physics change must be made twice |
| 9 | **Gym base seams bypassed via casts** | `GymEnemies._onRespawn` reaches into private `entities`/`playerBullets` and re-implements `GymFormationScene._respawnFormation`; `_onTogglePlayer` casts to mutate the base's private `player`/spawn coords | Duplicate respawn logic; fragile casts |
| 10 | **Restart/teardown parity** | `PlayScene._resetRunState` calls `effectsRegistry.reset()`; `GymFormationScene` only recreates the registry when the power-up layer is enabled, and never resets it on teardown, so `GymMinerals`/`GymEnemies` keep permanent effects across a restart | Stale effects after restart in gyms without field drops |
| 11 | **GymPlayer not on the shared control core** | `GymPlayer` extends `Phaser.Scene` and inlines the scheme→input mapping; no shared player tick | The "player" object is the one object with a genuinely separate code path in one gym |
| 12 | **No automated parity guard for the second tier** | The existing `definesMethod` guard (`CombatScene.equivalence.test.ts`) covers only the original eight methods; none of the shared helpers above are guarded, and the cross-scene equivalence test covers only a subset of behaviours | Future divergence is invisible until a user reports a bug |

- [ ] **AC1 — Each gap in the register has a single shared implementation.** Gaps 1–11 are closed by extracting the duplicated behaviour into the shared core/module or by consuming an existing shared hook; no production scene re-implements a shared behaviour. Verified by the extended duplicate-body guard and by prototype-identity assertions.
- [ ] **AC2 — Behavioural gaps are closed (or explicitly documented as intentional).** Every behavioural difference identified in gaps 1–11 (P9 magnet in formation gyms, P4 notice, per-type pickup cues, boss-in-`tick`, boss teleport avoidance, teleport gating, hold overflow, restart effect reset, GymPlayer input) is either made identical to the game or recorded as an intentional, approved difference in the epic description and the relevant child.

- [ ] **AC7 — Full project test suite passes.** The complete suite (`/skill:test`, `npm test`) passes with zero failures and no newly-flaky tests.

- **Single source of truth:** extract genuinely shared behaviour; do not trade one duplication for another. A shared module must not force game-only concerns (score, waves, lives) into gyms, nor gym-only concerns (editor, fixed formations) into the game.
- **Minimum churn / surgical:** match existing style; do not delete unrelated dead code (report it instead).
- **Preserve public/test seams** (e.g. `getBullets`, `advanceBullets`, `getDrops`, `getCollectAnimations`, `spawnDrop`, `triggerTeleport`, `getPlayerHitCount`, help/back handles).
- **Generics/type-safety:** the shared core is generic (`<TEnemy, TBullet, TDrop>`); additions must not weaken typing.
- **Determinism:** tests drive `tick(dt)`; shared behaviour must be driven by the supplied `dt` and the scene clock — no frame-count fake clocks.
- **UK English** in all written output and docs.
- **Gating:** implementation proceeds only through `/skill:implement`; this item does not authorise code changes.

- **Risk — over-abstraction.** Pushing gym-only features into the shared core couples the game to dev tooling. Mitigation: share behaviour only, keep features behind hooks/flags.
- **Risk — behaviour-change ambiguity.** Some divergences may be intentional. Mitigation: each is listed as an OPEN QUESTION below; the default assumption is "the game's behaviour is canonical" unless the producer says otherwise.

# Shared player-control step across all scenes

**Parent:** `AH-0MUII2FJ5007MDDA` (register gap 1 & 11).

## Summary

The sequence *input → tick weapon timers → apply P5 speed/fire-rate multipliers → physics → auto-fire* is re-implemented in `PlayScene.tick`, `GymFormationScene.tick`, `GymWeapons.tick`, `GymPowerUpsUtility.tick` and `GymPowerUpsCombat.tick`, and `GymPlayer.update` inlines the scheme→input mapping instead of the shared `_readPlayerInput`. Extract one `_tickPlayer(dt)` (and keep `_readPlayerInput`) in `CombatCoreScene` so every scene advances the player identically.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1** — `CombatCoreScene` owns a single `_tickPlayer(dt)` that performs, in the same order every frame: `tickWeaponTimers`, live `setSpeedMultiplier`/`setFireRateMultiplier` from the effects registry, `_readPlayerInput`→`setInput`, `physicsTick`, and `_autoFire`. `PlayScene`, `GymFormationScene`, `GymWeapons` and `GymPowerUpsUtility` call it instead of their local copy. Verified by prototype-identity assertions.
- [ ] **AC2** — `GymPlayer` consumes the shared input mapping (calls `_readPlayerInput` or an extracted shared input helper) and no longer inlines the `fourDirHandler`/`asteroidsHandler` branch. Verified by a source guard and by `GymPlayer.test.ts`.
- [ ] **AC3** — Timed-weapon expiry, P5 multipliers and auto-fire ordering are identical in the game and every gym for the same input and `dt`. Verified by a cross-scene equivalence test booting `PlayScene` and a gym, applying a P5 effect and asserting the same speed/fire-rate outcome.
- [ ] **AC4** — `GymPowerUpsCombat` no longer uses a fake fixed 16 ms clock for the player path; the player is advanced from the supplied `dt` (the enemy-clock fix is child #2).
- [ ] **AC5** — All existing scene suites pass unchanged; the repo-wide duplicate-body guard covers `_tickPlayer`.
- [ ] **AC6** — All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, `README.md` and `docs/Game Design Document.md` §6.4.
- [ ] **AC7** — Full project test suite must pass with the new changes.


**Parent-AC traceability** (implements parent `AH-0MUII2FJ5007MDDA`):
- [ ] **Parent-AC traceability (AC1)** — [ ] **AC1 — Each gap in the register has a single shared implementation.** Gaps 1–11 are closed by extracting the duplicated behaviour into the shared core/module or by consuming an existing shared hook; no production scene re-implements a shared behaviour. Verified by the extended duplicate-body guard and by prototype-identity assertions.
- [ ] **Parent-AC traceability (AC2)** — [ ] **AC2 — Behavioural gaps are closed (or explicitly documented as intentional).** Every behavioural difference identified in gaps 1–11 (P9 magnet in formation gyms, P4 notice, per-type pickup cues, boss-in-`tick`, boss teleport avoidance, teleport gating, hold overflow, restart effect reset, GymPlayer input) is either made identical to the game or recorded as an intentional, approved difference in the epic description and the relevant child.
- [ ] **Parent-AC traceability (AC3)** — [ ] **AC3 — Cross-scene equivalence for every object.** Automated tests boot both `PlayScene` and each gym and assert identical outcomes for the player, each enemy archetype, asteroids (incl. split), the boss, minerals (collection/hold/choice), power-ups (spawn/lifecycle/collect/magnet/bomb/cues) and projectiles under the same input and `dt`.
- [ ] **Parent-AC traceability (AC5)** — [ ] **AC5 — No behaviour regression in the game.** `PlayScene` behaviour and all existing tests remain green; any change to game behaviour is called out explicitly in the epic and approved as canonical.
- [ ] **Parent-AC traceability (AC6)** — [ ] **AC6 — Documentation.** `docs/Game Design Document.md` §6.4, `docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md`, the gym docstrings and `README.md` describe the shared behaviour modules, the hooks a gym implements, and the constrained-feature (not divergent-code) nature of gyms.
- [ ] **Parent-AC traceability (AC7)** — [ ] **AC7 — Full project test suite passes.** The complete suite (`/skill:test`, `npm test`) passes with zero failures and no newly-flaky tests.

## Key Files

- `src/scenes/PlayScene.ts`, `src/scenes/gym/core/GymFormationScene.ts`, `src/scenes/gym/GymWeapons.ts`, `src/scenes/gym/GymPowerUpsUtility.ts`, `src/scenes/gym/GymPowerUpsCombat.ts`, `src/scenes/gym/GymPlayer.ts` — consume the shared step.

# Epic: Realistic demo/attract bot framework + playtester telemetry

## Problem

The shipped attract/demo bot (AH-0MUX2NENC008AHOQ and its follow-ups) is a
per-frame priority ladder with a reaction-time governor bolted on. It has no
commitment, no forward model, no aim/fire reasoning and no way to learn from
human play, so it reads as random and cannot be tuned into competence. We need
a **maintainable bot framework** that plays competently and human-like, adapts
to new content (enemies, power-ups, weapons) without a rewrite, can be re-run
headless for reproducible evaluation, and is backed by **telemetry** gathered
both from our own recordings and from production playtesters.

## Goals / user stories

- **As the maintainer**, I can re-run the bot headless on a fixed seed and get
  reproducible results, so I can improve it safely.
- **As the maintainer**, I can add a new enemy / power-up / weapon and have the
  bot handle it through configuration, without touching the core.
- **As the maintainer**, I can record human play and analyse it (reaction
  times, target choices, engagement distances, dodge behaviour) to tune and
  evaluate the bot.
- **As the maintainer**, I can enable opt-in telemetry in production and gather
  playtester data (state + input + events) to improve the bot and the game.
- **As a player**, I see an attract/demo mode that looks like a competent
  player.

## Design overview

- **Determinism.** A per-run **seed** drives all gameplay RNG (wave/spawn/
  timing) so a run is reproducible and the bot can be evaluated same-seed.
- **Telemetry.** A **versioned, consent-gated, pluggable** pipeline. Records
  are per-tick state + input + discrete events, tagged with the run seed and a
  schema version. Sinks: a local JSONL dev sink and a production remote sink.
  No PII; **disabled by default in production**, opt-in only.
- **Bot framework.** A world model (from `BotSnapshot`), a **registry of
  goals/behaviours**, a **utility selector with commitment/hysteresis**, a
  behaviour-tree executor, and predictive **dodge/aim** behaviours.
  Content-specific parameters live in a **config/registry** so new content is
  data, not code.
- **Evaluation.** Same-seed bot-vs-human runs, metrics, A/B comparisons and
  side-by-side clips.
- **Style matching (later).** Fit parameters or train a policy from recorded
  telemetry once the competent bot exists.

## Epic acceptance criteria

- **AC1:** Runs are reproducible from a seed; the seed is recorded in
  telemetry; a headless runner executes the bot for N ticks on a seed and
  produces a deterministic report.
- **AC2:** Telemetry is a pluggable framework with a documented, versioned
  schema, disabled by default in production and opt-in consent-gated; it
  records per-tick state + input + events with the seed and is a no-op when
  disabled.
- **AC3:** The bot is a structured framework (world model + goal/behaviour
  registry + committed selection + predictive dodge/aim), not a per-frame
  priority ladder; new enemies/power-ups/weapons are handled via config with
  tests.
- **AC4:** The competent bot completes representative runs with human-like
  behaviour (goal commitment, no suicide, human cadence) and passes an
  evaluation report (survival, minerals/min, targets engaged, dodges).
- **AC5:** Human play can be recorded and analysed offline, and a replay/ghost
  viewer compares bot vs human on the same seed.
- **AC6:** Production telemetry can be enabled by a playtester via an explicit
  opt-in, with privacy documentation and no PII.
- **AC7:** All documentation is updated (framework, extension guide, telemetry
  schema/privacy); full suite, typecheck and build pass.

## Out of scope (this epic)

- A fully style-matched clone of a specific player (style matching is an
  early-phase deliverable; full fidelity is a later follow-up).
- Server-side ML training infrastructure or online multiplayer.
- CI wiring of the capture/eval jobs (follow-up once the harness exists).

## Children (dependency order)

1. Deterministic run seeding + seed plumbing.
2. Telemetry framework (versioned schema, pluggable sinks, consent flag).
3. Game telemetry instrumentation (per-tick state + events).
4. Dev recording, analysis and replay/ghost tooling.
5. Bot framework core (world model, goal/behaviour registry, committed policy,
   content config).
6. Structured competent bot (utility goals + behaviour tree + predictive
   dodge/aim).
7. Content-adaptive configuration for enemies, power-ups and weapons.
8. Same-seed evaluation harness (metrics, A/B, side-by-side clips).
9. Style matching from telemetry (parameter fitting / imitation).
10. Production telemetry (opt-in consent, privacy, remote sink, docs).

## Related work

Builds on AH-0MUX2NENC008AHOQ (Smart capture bot) and its follow-ups
AH-0MUXXQ1MN002RXGB (human-like input) and AH-0MUXYOV4C008MV0L (movement
goals). Supersedes the per-frame priority-ladder design.

# Screen Action Intensity Tracking and Analysis

**Work item:** Screen action intensity tracking and analysis (AH-0MUZCSJXQ004TREN)
**Type:** task (research/decision) · **Priority:** high · **Stage:** intake

> **Headline:** AI_Hell has no recorded measure of on-screen action. This work item researches how games have tracked action/excitement intensity, decides on an approach (with a refined weighed scoring model and output schema), and creates the implementation epic — it makes no runtime changes itself.

## Problem statement

AI_Hell has no way to measure, record or reason about how much action is on
screen during a run. Designers cannot see where a run is boring or
unreadably crowded, pacing systems have no signal to react to, and the
existing gameplay-capture pipeline cannot automatically identify exciting
moments for highlight clips. We need a recorded, timestamped measure of
on-screen activity — and a researched decision on how best to compute it.

## Users (example user stories)

- **As a game designer**, I can view a time-series of on-screen action
  intensity for a run, so I can evaluate pacing and identify boring or
  over-crowded segments.
- **As a game designer**, I can feed action-intensity data into future pacing
  / adaptive-difficulty work so the game maintains engaging but readable
  gameplay.
- **As a video editor**, I can use action-intensity timestamps to
  automatically select highlight clips from captured gameplay.
- **As a player**, action tracking does not affect gameplay behaviour or
  frame rate, and is not shipped enabled in production unless opted in.
- **As a maintainer**, the recording reuses the shared telemetry pipeline
  rather than introducing a parallel, drifting instrumentation path.

## Acceptance criteria

1. **Research & decision document exists.** A document under `docs/dev/`
   surveys how action/excitement intensity has been tracked in games (past
   and present) and compares **at least three** approaches, with a clear,
   justified recommendation for AI_Hell.
2. **Scoring model defined and refined.** The document defines the object
   categories, a weighed scoring formula (refining the seed weights:
   player/enemy bullets 1, enemies 2, enemy explosions 2, player explosions
   20, asteroids 1, upgrades 1, boss explosions 5, bosses 5), and explains
   each weight's rationale. It states how the score is aggregated, sampled
   and normalised.
3. **Output format specified.** The document defines the recorded artefact:
   its schema (timestamp, score, per-category breakdown, run seed, schema
   version), sample rate, file location/format, and how it joins to captured
   video for highlight selection.
4. **Telemetry integration stated.** The document states how the chosen
   approach integrates with / depends on the telemetry epic
   (AH-0MUY089KR003F8S4) and its instrumentation child
   (AH-0MUY08VVQ007HSSH), and confirms the telemetry work item remains at
   least `high` priority.
5. **Implementation epic created.** A follow-up implementation **epic** is
   created as a **sibling** of this item (linked via
   `discovered-from:AH-0MUZCSJXQ004TREN`), so this research item can close
   once the decision is recorded without waiting for implementation. The new
   epic records its own ACs and dependency on the telemetry items.
6. **All related documentation is updated** to reflect the changes, including
   code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries.
7. **Full project test suite must pass** with the new changes.

## Constraints

- **No gameplay change (this item).** This work item is research + decision +
  epic creation only; it must not change runtime behaviour.
- **Reuse, do not duplicate.** The existing shared core
  (`src/scenes/core/`) and telemetry effort are the canonical integration
  points; a parallel instrumentation path is prohibited by the repo
  gym↔game parity convention.
- **Cheap and bounded.** Any eventual per-tick computation must be
  O(entities) with negligible overhead, and must be a no-op when disabled.
- **Determinism-friendly.** The metric should be a pure function of scene
  state where possible, so it is reproducible from a seeded run.
- **Dev/opt-in gating.** Recording must not enter the shipped production
  bundle unless explicitly enabled (mirroring the capture pipeline's
  `import.meta.env.DEV` pattern).

## Existing state

- No action-intensity or excitement metric exists in `src/`.
- The telemetry epic (AH-0MUY089KR003F8S4) plans a **versioned, consent-gated,
  pluggable** pipeline recording per-tick state + input + discrete events,
  tagged with run seed and schema version. Its instrumentation child
  AH-0MUY08VVQ007HSSH defines a compact state vector built from the existing
  `BotSnapshot` builder — the natural place to add an `actionIntensity`
  field.
- Entities are already tracked in the shared core:
  `Player`, `Boss`, `Asteroid`, `CombatEnemyEntity`, `PlayerBullet`,
  `CombatEnemyBullet`, `CombatDrop`, plus player-explosion graphics in
  `CombatCoreScene.playerExplosions` and enemy/boss explosion VFX.
- The gameplay-capture pipeline (`docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md`) already
  records full runs to WebM and probes "non-trivial" content via non-black
  pixel fraction, colour variety and inter-frame motion — a coarse,
  video-only proxy for action that this work would replace/augment with a
  game-logic signal.
- A pure dev-scenario resolver (`src/core/devScenario.ts`) and a dev-gated
  run-ended signal (`src/core/runEndedSignal.ts`) already exist as precedents
  for dev-only game→tooling signals.

## Desired change

Produce a decision document that selects an approach, then create the
implementation epic. The document must cover:

- **Prior art / research** (see below).
- **Alternative approaches** compared against weighted object counting.
- **A refined scoring model** with per-weight rationale.
- **The recorded artefact's schema and join semantics** for video editing.
- **Integration with the telemetry pipeline** and gym↔game parity.

## Research: prior art (seed for the decision document)

The following is the intake research summary; the decision document must
verify and expand it with citations.

### Pacing / director systems

- **Left 4 Dead AI Director (Valve, 2008)** — the canonical example. Computes
  a smoothed per-player *stress* / *intensity* from health, damage taken,
  being-attacked state and proximity, then drives horde spawns, item
  placement and adaptive music with a **build-up/release** curve. See
  Booth, *The AI Systems of Left 4 Dead* (2009).
- **Alien: Isolation (2014)**, **Back 4 Blood**, **Deep Rock Galactic** —
  descendants of the director pattern; adapt pressure to observed
  player state rather than a fixed script.
- **Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment (DDA)** — Resident Evil 4, God Hand,
  Mario Kart rubber-band AI: adapt challenge from performance metrics.

### Player-experience / affective modelling

- **Player Experience Modelling (PEM)** — Yannakakis & Hallam (2007/2009)
  model satisfaction/arousal from gameplay metrics and physiological signals
  (GSR, HR, EEG); used for real-time adaptation.
- **Psychophysiology of games** — Ravaja et al. (2006), Mandryk et al.
  (2006): event-locked EDA/ECG/EMG as ground truth for "excitement".
  Accurate but invasive; useful as *calibration* data, not runtime.

### Domain-specific density metrics

- **Bullet-hell / shmup design** — bullet density (bullets on screen, or
  bullets/second) is a standard, quantitative difficulty axis (e.g.
  Touhou/Danmakufu tooling). Directly analogous to the proposed weighted
  object count.
- **Rhythm games** — note density (notes/second) drives the star-rating
  difficulty model (osu!, StepMania).
- **RTS / esports** — Actions Per Minute (APM), supply/unit counts as
  engagement proxies.
- **Adaptive/interactive music** — Wwise/FMOD expose an *Intensity* parameter
  that scales layered music from game state; a mature, shipped precedent for
  a single scalar "action" value driving output.

### Video / highlight detection

- **NVIDIA ShadowPlay Highlights / Medal / Twitch Clips** — mostly use
  game-specific event hooks (kills) and/or audio-loudness and motion spikes.
- **Film/edit research** — action/edit intensity from shot length, motion
  vectors and audio RMS; the capture pipeline's existing probe is a crude
  version of this.

### Physics / rendering proxies

- **Kinetic-energy metrics** — sum of speed²·mass over entities as a motion
  proxy.
- **Screen entropy / edge density** — renderer-side pixel statistics; cheap
  to derive from a recording, not from game logic.

## Alternative approaches (to be compared in the decision document)

1. **Weighted on-screen object count (seed proposal).** Sum of live entity
   counts × per-type weight, sampled per tick, timestamped. Deterministic,
   cheap, reuses the telemetry state vector; weak at capturing *bursty*
   action and *threat*.
2. **Event-window intensity.** Count discrete events (shots fired, hits,
   kills, explosions, pickups) in a sliding window; captures bursts and
   moment-to-moment change, but not steady crowding.
3. **Player-stress model (AI-Director style).** Derive intensity from player
   health, recent damage, incoming-bullet proximity and nearest-enemy
   distance — measures *perceived* pressure, not raw population.
4. **Physics/motion proxy.** Sum of entity speeds (or kinetic energy) +
   projectile count; captures motion but treats harmless drift and
   threatening movement alike.
5. **Rendering/AV proxy.** Pixel entropy / edge density and audio loudness;
   ideal for post-hoc video analysis, unavailable to in-game pacing.
6. **Hybrid layered metric (likely recommendation).** Weighted object count
   (layer 1) + event window (layer 2) combined into a normalised,
   exponentially smoothed `actionIntensity` scalar plus a `burstiness`
   derivative — then persisted as a versioned time series feeding both
   pacing and video-editing consumers.

## Key Files (predicted)

- `docs/dev/action-intensity.md` — **new**; the research + decision document
  this work item delivers.
- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — reference/cross-link for the scoring model
  and pacing rationale.
- `src/scenes/core/CombatCoreScene.ts` / `CombatScene.ts` — shared entity
  registries (player bullets, enemy bullets, drops, enemies, explosions) that
  a future counter would read.
- `src/ai/` (world model / `BotSnapshot` builder) — predicted reuse point for
  the per-tick state vector.
- `src/core/runEndedSignal.ts`, `src/core/devScenario.ts` — precedents for a
  dev-gated game→tooling signal.
- `docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md`, `scripts/capture-gameplay.mjs` — the video
  consumer that would join timestamps to captured WebM.
- `docs/ENEMY_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md` §5.1 — gym↔game parity convention
  any implementation must follow.

## Related work

- **AH-0MUY089KR003F8S4** — Realistic demo/attract bot framework + playtester
  telemetry (parent epic; telemetry infrastructure this builds on).
- **AH-0MUY08VVQ007HSSH** — Game telemetry instrumentation: per-tick state
  and events (child; `actionIntensity` field would live here).
- **AH-0MUY08VJ9006BHJO** — Telemetry framework: versioned schema, pluggable
  sinks, consent flag (child; provides the sink/schema for the time series).
- **AH-0MUY08W7Y004GATZ** — Dev recording, analysis and replay/ghost tooling
  (consumer of the recorded action series).
- **AH-0MUY08XLD009K4W4** — Same-seed evaluation harness (consumer for
  pacing/A-B metrics).
- **AH-0MUWMFF3C002WOBK** — Automated gameplay capture spike (video consumer;
  see `docs/dev/gameplay-capture.md`).
- **AH-0MUX2NENC008AHOQ** — Smart capture bot (emits the runs action
  intensity would be recorded against).

## Risks & assumptions

- **Risk — duplicate instrumentation (scope creep).** Building a standalone
  counter would drift from the telemetry pipeline; mitigated by making
  telemetry integration AC4 and mandating reuse.
- **Risk — weights are subjective.** The seed weights may not reflect
  perceived excitement; mitigated by making the model **tunable/config-driven**
  and documenting the rationale per weight, with event-window and stress
  signals as cross-checks.
- **Risk — metric ≠ excitement.** Object count is at best a *proxy*; the
  document must state this explicitly and recommend calibration against
  human ratings or physiological data before it drives difficulty.
- **Risk — performance / bundle impact.** Mitigated by O(entities), sampling,
  and dev/opt-in gating.
- **Risk — capture de-sync.** Joining the JSONL series to captured WebM
  timestamps needs a shared clock anchor; record a run-start timestamp/seed.
- **Assumption —** the telemetry epic's per-tick state recording
  (AH-0MUY08VVQ007HSSH) is the canonical integration point and remains
  `high` priority.
- **Assumption —** the metric is sampled, not stored per rendered frame, to
  bound file size (rate to be decided in the document, e.g. 10 Hz).
- **Scope-creep note:** pacing algorithms, ML excitement prediction and
  auto-editing are **consumers**, not deliverables of this item; captured as
  separate work items below if not already tracked.

## Appendix: Clarifying questions & answers

- **Q1: Scope of this work item — research + decision only, or include a
  prototype implementation?**
  Answer (operator, interactive reply): *"just the research + decision + epic
  creation"*. Source: interactive reply, 2026-10-08. → AC1, AC5, and the
  "no gameplay change" constraint.
- **Q2: Should action intensity be built on the telemetry pipeline
  (AH-0MUY089KR003F8S4) or standalone? Should the telemetry item's priority
  be raised?**
  Answer (operator, interactive reply): *"part of it, ensure the telemetry
  item is at least high priority"*. Source: interactive reply, 2026-10-08.
  Verified: telemetry epic AH-0MUY089KR003F8S4, framework
  AH-0MUY08VJ9006BHJO and instrumentation AH-0MUY08VVQ007HSSH are already
  `high`. → AC4 and the reuse constraint.
- **Q3: Should the research refine the seed scoring weights, or treat them
  as definitive?**
  Answer (operator, interactive reply): *"refining included"*. Source:
  interactive reply, 2026-10-08. → AC2.
